title: From Edge to HPC: Investigating Cross-Facility Data Streaming Architectures
problem: HPC datacenters must handle diverse data streaming patterns (edge sensors to HPC, inter-facility transfers) with varying latency and throughput requirements, but architectural trade-offs between directness, scalability, and deployment feasibility are poorly understood.
motivation: Scientific workflows increasingly require real-time data ingestion from edge devices and collaboration across computing facilities, demanding architectural guidance for streaming integration.
method: They tested three different architectures for moving data between facilities: Direct (straightforward connection), Proxied (routed through an intermediate server), and Managed Service (using a cloud service). They ran this evaluation on real HPC infrastructure—OLCF's Advanced Computing Ecosystem—using the DS2HPC framework and SciStream toolkit. They used synthetic workloads designed to mimic real scientific workflows to measure how each architecture performed.
key_novelty: This is the first time anyone has systematically measured how different cross-facility data-streaming designs (Direct, Proxied, and Managed Service approaches) perform on real production HPC systems.
contributions: Three streaming architectures: Direct (DTS), Proxied (PRS), Managed Service (MSS)
DS2HPC architectural framework and SciStream memory-to-memory toolkit
Measurement of throughput, latency, overhead across communication patterns
Performance characterization: DTS (minimal hops, high throughput), MSS (high overhead), PRS (scalable middle ground)
Production deployment on OLCF ACE infrastructure
limitations: Evaluation limited to synthetic workloads; real-world workflow patterns may differ; specific to OLCF ACE infrastructure; generalization to other facilities unclear.
